analysis.one_liner: Strengthens union organizing rights with penalties for employer intimidation and binding arbitration for first contracts.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a single cosponsor and died in a House subcommittee in 2009 without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have changed federal labor law in three main ways for workplaces with 20 or more employees. It would have forced bargaining to a conclusion: if a newly certified union and employer could not agree on a first contract, after two 120-day periods the dispute would go to binding arbitration, meaning an arbitrator would impose a contract. It would have required employers to give unions equal access to the workplace to campaign before a union election, and to disclose their planned anti-union campaign activities. And it would have toughened penalties for employers who fire or threaten workers during organizing drives, adding triple back pay and civil fines up to $20,000 per violation, with priority investigation of those charges.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers trying to organize a union and unions themselves. Under current law, an employer can campaign against a union with full workplace access while the union cannot, and can fire organizers with remedies that often arrive years later and amount to back pay only. This bill would have given unions equal campaign access, doubled-plus-one back pay for fired workers, new fines for willful violations, and a guaranteed end to first-contract stalemates through arbitration.

how_it_helps.text: If a first contract is not reached within 120 days of bargaining and 120 days more of mediation, a Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service arbitration panel would impose a binding contract lasting at least 18 months, ending what can be years of stalemate.

Employers would have to give the union equal access to the workplace to campaign for recognition, including the same number of meetings, announcements, signs, and literature, and failing to do so would itself be an unfair labor practice.

Employers who fire or discriminate against workers during organizing drives would owe back pay plus double that amount as liquidated damages, and willful or repeated violators could face civil penalties up to $20,000 per violation.
Charges that an employer fired or threatened workers during a union drive would get priority investigation, so cases would not sit at the back of the line for years.

analysis.who_pays: Employers, especially those that actively oppose union drives. They would face new financial exposure (triple back pay and $20,000 fines), a duty to disclose and share their campaign access with unions, and the risk of having contract terms set by an arbitrator rather than negotiated.

drawbacks.text: Binding arbitration means that if negotiations stall, an outside arbitrator—not the employer or the union—would write the contract terms, which critics argue substitutes government-imposed terms for genuine bargaining.

The equal-access provision would force employers to reveal their planned campaign activities in advance and to hand over workplace access to a union, which employers viewed as tilting elections and as a burden particularly for smaller companies with 20 or more employees.

The new penalties—double liquidated damages on top of back pay and fines up to $20,000 per violation—would raise the cost of doing business for employers found in violation, costs that could be passed on in prices or hiring.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers who want a union, the gains are substantial: real penalties for firing organizers, a fairer campaign, and no more open-ended first-contract stalemates. The genuine cost falls on employers, who lose both money and unilateral control over the campaign and the eventual contract. The arbitration mechanism is the most contested piece—imposing a contract after a fixed clock removes the employer's ability to simply wait a union out, but it also substitutes a third party's judgment for negotiation. Weighing it honestly, this is a deliberate rebalancing of union elections and first contracts toward workers, paid for almost entirely by employers that contest organizing.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, sent to the House Education and Labor Committee, then parked in a subcommittee, and sat there until the Congress ended with no hearing, no vote, and not even one cosponsor.

narrative.text: Rep. Joe Sestak (D-PA) introduced the National Labor Relations Modernization Act on March 5, 2009.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor the day it was introduced.
On April 29, 2009, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions—its last recorded action.
The bill attracted no cosponsors at any point.
No further action was taken before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, so the bill died in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers, especially those that fight union organizing drives, are better off because the bill died: they keep the current rules under which union elections face no equal-access requirement, firing an organizer carries only back-pay liability with no added damages, and first-contract negotiations can stall indefinitely with no arbitration to force an outcome. Workers seeking to organize lost the strengthened protections entirely.

for.name: Rep. Joe Sestak
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only supporter in Congress; no member signed on as a cosponsor.

against.name: Rep. George Miller
against.role: Chair, House Education and Labor Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled committee action on the bill; it was referred to his committee on March 5, 2009, passed to a subcommittee on April 29, and never reported out.

against.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce and employer groups
against.what_they_did: Fiercely opposed the family of 2009 labor-law bills that would strengthen union organizing and impose first-contract arbitration, running a major campaign against them; this bill contained the same core elements.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill had zero cosponsors, so there is no record of how the parties would have lined up; it had only a single Democratic sponsor.

industries.industry: Employers, especially nonunion companies that contest organizing drives
industries.note: The bill would have exposed them to triple back pay and fines up to $20,000 per violation for firing or threatening organizers, required them to share campaign access with unions, and allowed arbitrators to impose first contracts. Their gain from the bill's death is the public's loss of those worker protections.
Unions would gain equal campaign access, faster first contracts via arbitration, and stronger enforcement backing—changes that help the workers unions represent.

industries.industry: Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service and labor arbitrators
industries.note: Every stalled first-contract negotiation would have generated a new mediation and arbitration proceeding, expanding their caseload and role.
